claim: Circulating lactate is a fuel source for liver metabolism.
source: Circulating lactate is a fuel source for liver metabolism but may exacerbate metabolic diseases such as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: Circulating lactate may exacerbate metabolic diseases such as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).
source: Circulating lactate is a fuel source for liver metabolism but may exacerbate metabolic diseases such as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis or speculation about lactate's role in NASH.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of lactate transporter monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) in mice reportedly promotes resistance to hepatic steatosis and inflammation.
source: Indeed, haploinsufficiency of lactate transporter monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) in mice reportedly promotes resistance to hepatic steatosis and inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature, indicated by 'reportedly'.

claim: Stellate cell MCT1KO (AAV-Lrat-Cre) attenuated liver type 1 collagen protein expression in MCT1fl/fl mice on a choline-deficient, high-fat NASH diet.
source: Stellate cell MCT1KO (AAV-Lrat-Cre) attenuated liver type 1 collagen protein expression and caused a downward trend in trichrome staining.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Stellate cell MCT1KO caused a downward trend in trichrome staining in MCT1fl/fl mice on a choline-deficient, high-fat NASH diet.
source: Stellate cell MCT1KO (AAV-Lrat-Cre) attenuated liver type 1 collagen protein expression and caused a downward trend in trichrome staining.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: MCT1 depletion in cultured human LX2 stellate cells diminished collagen 1 protein expression.
source: MCT1 depletion in cultured human LX2 stellate cells also diminished collagen 1 protein expression.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from in vitro studies.

claim: Tetra-ethylenglycol-cholesterol (Chol)-conjugated siRNAs enter all hepatic cell types.
source: Tetra-ethylenglycol-cholesterol (Chol)-conjugated siRNAs, which enter all hepatic cell types, and hepatocyte-selective tri-N-acetyl galactosamine (GN)-conjugated siRNAs were then used to evaluate MCT1 function in a genetically obese NASH mouse model.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the Chol-conjugated siRNAs used in the study.

claim: Tri-N-acetyl galactosamine (GN)-conjugated siRNAs are hepatocyte-selective.
source: Tetra-ethylenglycol-cholesterol (Chol)-conjugated siRNAs, which enter all hepatic cell types, and hepatocyte-selective tri-N-acetyl galactosamine (GN)-conjugated siRNAs were then used to evaluate MCT1 function in a genetically obese NASH mouse model.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the GN-conjugated siRNAs used in the study.

claim: MCT1 silencing by Chol-siRNA decreased liver collagen 1 levels in a genetically obese NASH mouse model.
source: MCT1 silencing by Chol-siRNA decreased liver collagen 1 levels, while hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion by AAV-TBG-Cre or by GN-siRNA unexpectedly increased collagen 1 and total fibrosis without effect on triglyceride accumulation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion by AAV-TBG-Cre unexpectedly increased collagen 1 and total fibrosis in a genetically obese NASH mouse model.
source: MCT1 silencing by Chol-siRNA decreased liver collagen 1 levels, while hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion by AAV-TBG-Cre or by GN-siRNA unexpectedly increased collagen 1 and total fibrosis without effect on triglyceride accumulation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion by GN-siRNA unexpectedly increased collagen 1 and total fibrosis in a genetically obese NASH mouse model.
source: MCT1 silencing by Chol-siRNA decreased liver collagen 1 levels, while hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion by AAV-TBG-Cre or by GN-siRNA unexpectedly increased collagen 1 and total fibrosis without effect on triglyceride accumulation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion by AAV-TBG-Cre or by GN-siRNA had no effect on triglyceride accumulation in a genetically obese NASH mouse model.
source: MCT1 silencing by Chol-siRNA decreased liver collagen 1 levels, while hepatocyte-selective MCT1 depletion by AAV-TBG-Cre or by GN-siRNA unexpectedly increased collagen 1 and total fibrosis without effect on triglyceride accumulation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Stellate cell lactate transporter MCT1 significantly contributes to liver fibrosis through increased collagen 1 protein expression in vitro and in vivo.
source: These findings demonstrate that stellate cell lactate transporter MCT1 significantly contributes to liver fibrosis through increased collagen 1 protein expression in vitro and in vivo, while hepatocyte MCT1 appears not to be an attractive therapeutic target for NASH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Hepatocyte MCT1 appears not to be an attractive therapeutic target for NASH.
source: These findings demonstrate that stellate cell lactate transporter MCT1 significantly contributes to liver fibrosis through increased collagen 1 protein expression in vitro and in vivo, while hepatocyte MCT1 appears not to be an attractive therapeutic target for NASH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased fibrosis with hepatocyte-specific MCT1 depletion.

claim: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common chronic liver disease, afflicting over a quarter of the world's population.
source: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common chronic liver disease, afflicting over a quarter of the world's population.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Younossi et al., 2016 and Estes et al., 2018.

claim: NAFLD describes a spectrum of liver diseases ranging from simple steatosis to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).
source: It describes a spectrum of liver diseases ranging from simple steatosis to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) (Younossi et al., 2016; Estes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Younossi et al., 2016 and Estes et al., 2018.

claim: Steatosis is considered relatively benign as lifestyle modifications can reverse fatty liver to a healthy condition.
source: Steatosis is considered relatively benign as lifestyle modifications can reverse fatty liver to a healthy condition.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: NASH is characterized by severe steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis.
source: On the other hand, NASH is characterized by severe steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Severe fibrotic stages of NASH can develop into permanent liver damage, and the disease can progress to cirrhosis and hepatoma.
source: Severe fibrotic stages of NASH can develop into permanent liver damage, and the disease can progress to cirrhosis and hepatoma.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: NASH is a leading cause for liver transplantation.
source: Currently, NASH is a leading cause for liver transplantation, and there is no FDA-approved therapeutic for NASH (Estes et al., 2018; Alexander et al., 2019; Diehl and Day, 2017; Friedman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Estes et al., 2018; Alexander et al., 2019; Diehl and Day, 2017; Friedman et al., 2018.

claim: There is no FDA-approved therapeutic for NASH.
source: Currently, NASH is a leading cause for liver transplantation, and there is no FDA-approved therapeutic for NASH (Estes et al., 2018; Alexander et al., 2019; Diehl and Day, 2017; Friedman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Estes et al., 2018; Alexander et al., 2019; Diehl and Day, 2017; Friedman et al., 2018.

claim: NASH is closely associated with the hallmarks of type 2 diabetes and obesity, including chronic overnutrition, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia.
source: Since NASH is closely associated with the hallmarks of type 2 diabetes and obesity, including chronic overnutrition, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia, it is likely that substrate overload to the liver contributes to its cause (Friedman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Friedman et al., 2018.

claim: Substrate overload to the liver likely contributes to the cause of NASH.
source: Since NASH is closely associated with the hallmarks of type 2 diabetes and obesity, including chronic overnutrition, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia, it is likely that substrate overload to the liver contributes to its cause (Friedman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Friedman et al., 2018.

claim: NAFLD and NASH patients display hyperactive liver tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle flux due to an overabundance of upstream metabolites.
source: Accordingly, NAFLD and NASH patients display hyperactive liver tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle flux due to an overabundance of upstream metabolites (García-Ruiz and Fernández-Checa, 2018; Sunny et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to García-Ruiz and Fernández-Checa, 2018; Sunny et al., 2017.

claim: Lowering substrate influx to the liver is a promising strategy to prevent and possibly alleviate steatosis and NASH.
source: These findings suggest that lowering substrate influx to the liver is a promising strategy to prevent and possibly alleviate steatosis and NASH.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited findings about hyperactive TCA cycle flux.

claim: Human subjects with type 2 diabetes and obesity reportedly have increased plasma lactate levels.
source: Human subjects with type 2 diabetes and obesity reportedly have increased plasma lactate levels (Lovejoy et al., 1992; Crawford et al., 2010; Juraschek et al., 2013a; Juraschek et al., 2013b; DiGirolamo et al., 1992; Sabater et al., 2014; Jansson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lactate is produced and released into the circulation when cellular glycolytic flux surpasses mitochondrial oxidative capacity.
source: Lactate is produced and released into the circulation when cellular glycolytic flux surpasses mitochondrial oxidative capacity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Lactate is now recognized as a primary fuel for the TCA cycle in liver and thus an essential energy source.
source: Once considered to be simply a metabolic waste product, lactate is now recognized as a primary fuel for the TCA cycle in liver and thus an essential energy source (Hui et al., 2017; Rabinowitz and Enerbäck, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hui et al., 2017; Rabinowitz and Enerbäck, 2020.

claim: Lactate is a critical regulator that contributes to whole-body energy homeostasis.
source: Additionally, it is a critical regulator that contributes to whole-body energy homeostasis (Brooks, 2020; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brooks, 2020; Li et al., 2022.

claim: Under physiological conditions, cellular lactate levels are tightly controlled by monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs).
source: Under physiological conditions, cellular lactate levels are tightly controlled by monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: MCTs are members of the solute carrier 16A (SLC16A) family, which are proton-coupled transmembrane protein transporters.
source: MCTs are members of the solute carrier 16A (SLC16A) family, which are proton-coupled transmembrane protein transporters.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Among 14 MCT isoforms, only MCTs 1–4 have been shown to transport monocarboxylate molecules such as lactate, pyruvate, short-chain fatty acids, and ketone bodies.
source: Among 14 MCT isoforms, only MCTs 1–4 have been shown to transport monocarboxylate molecules such as lactate, pyruvate, short-chain fatty acids, and ketone bodies (Felmlee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Felmlee et al., 2020.

claim: MCT1 is denoted as a primary lactate transporter as it is the most widely distributed MCT isoform in various metabolic tissues and has a high affinity for lactate.
source: Notably, MCT1 is denoted as a primary lactate transporter as it is the most widely distributed MCT isoform in various metabolic tissues and has a high affinity for lactate, maintaining basal cellular homeostasis according to transmembrane lactate gradients (Li et al., 2022; Halestrap, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2022; Halestrap, 2013.

claim: MCT1 maintains basal cellular homeostasis according to transmembrane lactate gradients.
source: Notably, MCT1 is denoted as a primary lactate transporter as it is the most widely distributed MCT isoform in various metabolic tissues and has a high affinity for lactate, maintaining basal cellular homeostasis according to transmembrane lactate gradients (Li et al., 2022; Halestrap, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2022; Halestrap, 2013.

claim: MCT1 haploinsufficiency in mice reduces MCT1 protein levels to nearly half in major metabolic tissues such as liver, brain, and white adipose tissues.
source: Reportedly, MCT1 haploinsufficiency in mice reduces MCT1 protein levels to nearly half in major metabolic tissues such as liver, brain, and white adipose tissues, and these mice are resistant to diet-induced obesity and liver steatosis and inflammation (Lengacher et al., 2013; Carneiro et al., 2017; Hadjihambi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lengacher et al., 2013; Carneiro et al., 2017; Hadjihambi et al., 2023.

claim: MCT1 haploinsufficient mice are resistant to diet-induced obesity and liver steatosis and inflammation.
source: Reportedly, MCT1 haploinsufficiency in mice reduces MCT1 protein levels to nearly half in major metabolic tissues such as liver, brain, and white adipose tissues, and these mice are resistant to diet-induced obesity and liver steatosis and inflammation (Lengacher et al., 2013; Carneiro et al., 2017; Hadjihambi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lengacher et al., 2013; Carneiro et al., 2017; Hadjihambi et al., 2023.

claim: The role of MCT1 in hypothalamus and adipose tissues in the phenotypes of MCT1 haploinsufficient mice was ruled out.
source: The role of MCT1 in hypothalamus and adipose tissues in these phenotypes was ruled out, as selective MCT1 depletion in those tissues either increased food intake and body weight (Elizondo-Vega et al., 2016) or enhanced systemic inflammation and insulin resistance (Lin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elizondo-Vega et al., 2016 and Lin et al., 2022.

claim: Selective MCT1 depletion in hypothalamus increased food intake and body weight.
source: The role of MCT1 in hypothalamus and adipose tissues in these phenotypes was ruled out, as selective MCT1 depletion in those tissues either increased food intake and body weight (Elizondo-Vega et al., 2016) or enhanced systemic inflammation and insulin resistance (Lin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Elizondo-Vega et al., 2016.

claim: Selective MCT1 depletion in adipose tissues enhanced systemic inflammation and insulin resistance.
source: The role of MCT1 in hypothalamus and adipose tissues in these phenotypes was ruled out, as selective MCT1 depletion in those tissues either increased food intake and body weight (Elizondo-Vega et al., 2016) or enhanced systemic inflammation and insulin resistance (Lin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2022.

claim: The question of which tissue or tissues are responsible for the phenotype of whole-body MCT1 haploinsufficiency is not solved.
source: Thus, the question of which tissue or tissues are responsible for the phenotype of whole-body MCT1 haploinsufficiency is not solved.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Hepatocytes account for the majority of liver cells and have high rates of lipogenesis and triglyceride (TG) accumulation.
source: Since hepatocytes account for the majority of liver cells and have high rates of lipogenesis and triglyceride (TG) accumulation, lactate levels governed by hepatocyte MCT1 could be involved in regulating steatosis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Hepatic stellate cells account for only 5–10% of the hepatic cell population.
source: On the other hand, while hepatic stellate cells account for only 5–10% of the hepatic cell population, they are the major cell type contributing to hepatic fibrogenesis (Wake, 1971; Mederacke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wake, 1971; Mederacke et al., 2013.

claim: Hepatic stellate cells are the major cell type contributing to hepatic fibrogenesis.
source: On the other hand, while hepatic stellate cells account for only 5–10% of the hepatic cell population, they are the major cell type contributing to hepatic fibrogenesis (Wake, 1971; Mederacke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wake, 1971; Mederacke et al., 2013.

claim: Fate tracing studies have revealed that 82–96% of myofibroblasts are derived from hepatic stellate cells.
source: Fate tracing studies have revealed that 82–96% of myofibroblasts are derived from hepatic stellate cells, which are liver-specific pericytes (Mederacke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mederacke et al., 2013.

claim: Hepatic stellate cells are liver-specific pericytes.
source: Fate tracing studies have revealed that 82–96% of myofibroblasts are derived from hepatic stellate cells, which are liver-specific pericytes (Mederacke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mederacke et al., 2013.

claim: During NASH progression, multiple liver injury signals stimulate the transition of vitamin A-storing quiescent hepatic stellate cells into fibrogenic, proliferative myofibroblasts that produce and secrete collagen fibers.
source: During NASH progression, multiple liver injury signals stimulate the transition of vitamin A-storing quiescent hepatic stellate cells into fibrogenic, proliferative myofibroblasts that produce and secrete collagen fibers (Trautwein et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2015; Puche et al., 2013; Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Trautwein et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2015; Puche et al., 2013; Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017.

claim: Healthy hepatic parenchyma is replaced with a collagen-rich extracellular matrix during NASH, turning the liver into a hardened and scarred tissue.
source: As a result, healthy hepatic parenchyma is replaced with a collagen-rich extracellular matrix, turning the liver into a hardened and scarred tissue (Mehal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehal et al., 2011.

claim: Major organ fibrosis is directly correlated with morbidity and mortality, contributing up to 45% of deaths in developed countries.
source: In general, major organ fibrosis is directly correlated with morbidity and mortality, contributing up to 45% of deaths in developed countries (Wynn, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wynn, 2008.

claim: Targeting activated hepatic stellate cells has become a major strategy in NASH therapeutics development.
source: Thus, targeting activated hepatic stellate cells has become a major strategy in NASH therapeutics development (Friedman et al., 2018; Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Friedman et al., 2018; Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017.

claim: The role of MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells activation or fibrogenesis has not been investigated.
source: However, the role of MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells activation or fibrogenesis has not been investigated.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: TGF-β1 stimulated expression of ACTA2 and collagen 1 isoform, COL1A1, by several folds in LX2 cells.
source: As expected, TGF-β1 stimulated expression of ACTA2 and collagen 1 isoform, COL1A1, by several folds (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: SLC16A1/MCT1 silencing significantly inhibited TGF-β1-stimulated ACTA2 mRNA expression in LX2 cells.
source: SLC16A1/MCT1 silencing significantly inhibited TGF-β1-stimulated ACTA2 mRNA expression as well as collagen 1 protein production (Figure 1B and C), indicating cell-autonomous functions of MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: SLC16A1/MCT1 silencing significantly inhibited TGF-β1-stimulated collagen 1 protein production in LX2 cells.
source: SLC16A1/MCT1 silencing significantly inhibited TGF-β1-stimulated ACTA2 mRNA expression as well as collagen 1 protein production (Figure 1B and C), indicating cell-autonomous functions of MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: MCT1 has cell-autonomous functions in hepatic stellate cells.
source: SLC16A1/MCT1 silencing significantly inhibited TGF-β1-stimulated ACTA2 mRNA expression as well as collagen 1 protein production (Figure 1B and C), indicating cell-autonomous functions of MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing direct effects of MCT1 silencing in LX2 cells.

claim: Chol-MCT1-2060 has an IC50 of 59.6 nM and achieves 87.2% knockdown of Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA in FL83B cells.
source: The two most potent Chol-MCT1-siRNA, Chol-MCT1-2060 (IC50: 59.6 nM, KD%: 87.2) and Chol-MCT1-3160 (IC50: 32.4 nM, KD%: 87.7) (Figure 2C), were evaluated for their inhibitory effect on MCT1 protein levels (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chol-MCT1-3160 has an IC50 of 32.4 nM and achieves 87.7% knockdown of Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA in FL83B cells.
source: The two most potent Chol-MCT1-siRNA, Chol-MCT1-2060 (IC50: 59.6 nM, KD%: 87.2) and Chol-MCT1-3160 (IC50: 32.4 nM, KD%: 87.7) (Figure 2C), were evaluated for their inhibitory effect on MCT1 protein levels (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chol-MCT1-3160 construct was chosen for further studies in vivo based on its IC50 value and silencing potency.
source: Based on its IC50 value and silencing potency, Chol-MCT1-3160 construct was chosen for further studies in vivo (Table 2).
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the experimental data.

claim: GN-conjugated, fully chemically modified MCT1-siRNA (GN-MCT1-siRNA) silenced Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA only in the hepatocyte fraction.
source: As expected, GN-conjugated, fully chemically modified MCT1-siRNA (GN-MCT1-siRNA) silenced Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA only in the hepatocyte fraction (Figure 3B–D), as GN binds to the asialoglycoprotein receptor primarily expressed in hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: GN binds to the asialoglycoprotein receptor primarily expressed in hepatocytes.
source: As expected, GN-conjugated, fully chemically modified MCT1-siRNA (GN-MCT1-siRNA) silenced Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA only in the hepatocyte fraction (Figure 3B–D), as GN binds to the asialoglycoprotein receptor primarily expressed in hepatocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about GN conjugates.

claim: Chol-MCT1-siRNA silenced Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA levels in all hepatic cell types.
source: On the other hand, Chol-MCT1-siRNA silenced Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA levels in all hepatic cell types (Figure 3E–G), as its cellular uptake is highly dependent on the non-specific, hydrophobic interaction between cholesterol and plasma membranes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Chol-MCT1-siRNA cellular uptake is highly dependent on the non-specific, hydrophobic interaction between cholesterol and plasma membranes.
source: On the other hand, Chol-MCT1-siRNA silenced Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA levels in all hepatic cell types (Figure 3E–G), as its cellular uptake is highly dependent on the non-specific, hydrophobic interaction between cholesterol and plasma membranes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cholesterol conjugates.

claim: The hepatic stellate cell fraction distinguishes GN-MCT1-siRNA from Chol-MCT1-siRNA in biodistribution, as only the latter silences Slc16a1/Mct1 in stellate cells.
source: Notably, the hepatic stellate cell fraction distinguishes GN-MCT1-siRNA from Chol-MCT1-siRNA in biodistribution, as only the latter silences Slc16a1/Mct1 in stellate cells (Figure 3C vs F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3C vs F.

claim: Both GN-MCT1-siRNA and Chol-MCT1-siRNA do not affect MCT1 levels in other major metabolic tissues.
source: We also confirmed that both GN-MCT1-siRNA and Chol-MCT1-siRNA do not affect MCT1 levels in other major metabolic tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J.

claim: Genetically obese ob/ob mice on a NASH-inducing Gubra Amylin NASH (GAN) diet normally develop severe steatosis from an early age but hardly develop fibrosis until fed the GAN diet.
source: We next investigated the effect of Chol-MCT1-siRNA on reversing severe steatosis in the genetically obese ob/ob mouse on a NASH-inducing Gubra Amylin NASH (GAN) diet (Yenilmez et al., 2022). These mice normally develop severe steatosis from an early age but hardly develop fibrosis until fed the GAN diet.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yenilmez et al., 2022.

claim: Chol-MCT1-siRNA administration resulted in more than 70% MCT1 protein depletion in ob/ob mice on GAN diet (77.99% silencing).
source: Hepatic MCT1 protein levels were visually monitored by MCT1-positive staining immunohistochemistry (Figure 4B and C), showing more than 70% MCT1 protein depletion (Chol-MCT1-siRNA: 77.99% and GN-MCT1-siRNA: 71.35% silencing).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: GN-MCT1-siRNA administration resulted in more than 70% MCT1 protein depletion in ob/ob mice on GAN diet (71.35% silencing).
source: Hepatic MCT1 protein levels were visually monitored by MCT1-positive staining immunohistochemistry (Figure 4B and C), showing more than 70% MCT1 protein depletion (Chol-MCT1-siRNA: 77.99% and GN-MCT1-siRNA: 71.35% silencing).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The silencing of MCT1 by siRNAs was Slc16a1/Mct1 selective, not depleting other isoforms such as Slc16a7/Mct2 and Slc16a3/Mct4.
source: The silencing was Slc16a1/Mct1 selective, not depleting other isoforms such as Slc16a7/Mct2 and Slc16a3/Mct4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: There was no surge in plasma lactate level after MCT1 depletion in the liver of ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: Importantly, there was no surge in plasma lactate level (Figure 4E), addressing the concern of potential lactic acidosis after MCT1 depletion in the liver, the major lactate-consuming tissue.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4E.

claim: GN-MCT1-siRNA administration led to a decrease in both food intake and body weight in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: Intriguingly, the GN-MCT1-siRNA administration led to a decrease in both food intake and body weight, while the Chol-MCT1-siRNA did not.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Chol-MCT1-siRNA administration did not lead to a decrease in food intake and body weight in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: Intriguingly, the GN-MCT1-siRNA administration led to a decrease in both food intake and body weight, while the Chol-MCT1-siRNA did not.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Neither Chol-MCT1-siRNA administration nor hepatocyte-specific MCT1KO improved glucose tolerance on the genetically obese NASH mouse model or a 12-week HFD-induced NAFLD model, respectively.
source: Neither Chol-MCT1-siRNA administration nor hepatocyte-specific MCT1KO improved glucose tolerance on the genetically obese NASH mouse model or a 12-week HFD-induced NAFLD model, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Neither GN-MCT1-siRNA nor Chol-MCT1-siRNA decreased total hepatic TG levels in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: The results showed that neither GN-MCT1-siRNA nor Chol-MCT1-siRNA decreased total hepatic TG levels (Figure 4H), although quantitative analysis of H&E images showed a small decrease in mean lipid droplet size and increased number of lipid droplets upon MCT1 silencing (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Quantitative analysis of H&E images showed a small decrease in mean lipid droplet size upon MCT1 silencing in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: The results showed that neither GN-MCT1-siRNA nor Chol-MCT1-siRNA decreased total hepatic TG levels (Figure 4H), although quantitative analysis of H&E images showed a small decrease in mean lipid droplet size and increased number of lipid droplets upon MCT1 silencing (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Quantitative analysis of H&E images showed increased number of lipid droplets upon MCT1 silencing in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: The results showed that neither GN-MCT1-siRNA nor Chol-MCT1-siRNA decreased total hepatic TG levels (Figure 4H), although quantitative analysis of H&E images showed a small decrease in mean lipid droplet size and increased number of lipid droplets upon MCT1 silencing (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Both GN-MCT1-siRNA and Chol-MCT1-siRNA strongly decreased the mRNA and protein levels related to representative DNL genes in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: Both GN-MCT1-siRNA and Chol-MCT1-siRNA strongly decreased the mRNA and protein levels related to representative DNL genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Both modes of hepatic MCT1 depletion inhibited expression of the upstream regulatory transcription factors SREBP1 and ChREBP in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: Intriguingly, both modes of hepatic MCT1 depletion also inhibited expression of the upstream regulatory transcription factors SREBP1 and ChREBP.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Phosphorylated AMPK (pAMPK) is known to inhibit SREBP nuclear translocation.
source: Because phosphorylated AMPK (pAMPK), an active form of AMPK, is known to inhibit SREBP nuclear translocation (Li et al., 2011) as well as the DNA binding activity of ChREBP (Kawaguchi et al., 2002), we evaluated pAMPK levels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Phosphorylated AMPK (pAMPK) is known to inhibit the DNA binding activity of ChREBP.
source: Because phosphorylated AMPK (pAMPK), an active form of AMPK, is known to inhibit SREBP nuclear translocation (Li et al., 2011) as well as the DNA binding activity of ChREBP (Kawaguchi et al., 2002), we evaluated pAMPK levels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kawaguchi et al., 2002.

claim: There was a significant increase in pAMPK levels and pAMPK/AMPK ratio in both GN-MCT1-siRNA and Chol-MCT1-siRNA injected groups of ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: As a result, there was a significant increase in pAMPK levels and pAMPK/AMPK ratio in both GN-MCT1-siRNA and Chol-MCT1-siRNA injected groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: Chol-MCT1-siRNA administration to ob/ob mice on GAN diet significantly reduced liver collagen 1 protein levels.
source: Consistent with the results in LX2 stellate cells (Figure 1), Chol-MCT1-siRNA administration to ob/ob mice on GAN diet significantly reduced liver collagen 1 protein levels (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Hepatocyte-specific GN-MCT1-siRNA enhanced the expression of type 1 collagen protein in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: Surprisingly, an opposite phenotype on collagen 1 protein expression was observed in response to administration of GN-MCT1-siRNA compared to Chol-MCT1-siRNA (Figure 5D and E). Hepatocyte-specific GN-MCT1-siRNA actually enhanced the expression of type 1 collagen protein in these experiments (Figure 5D and E), and this effect was also apparent at the mRNA expression level (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The effect of GN-MCT1-siRNA on collagen 1 expression was also apparent at the mRNA expression level in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: Surprisingly, an opposite phenotype on collagen 1 protein expression was observed in response to administration of GN-MCT1-siRNA compared to Chol-MCT1-siRNA (Figure 5D and E). Hepatocyte-specific GN-MCT1-siRNA actually enhanced the expression of type 1 collagen protein in these experiments (Figure 5D and E), and this effect was also apparent at the mRNA expression level (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5F.

claim: GN-MCT1-siRNA significantly enhanced Sirius Red positive areas in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: In line with collagen 1 mRNA and protein levels, GN-MCT1-siRNA significantly enhanced Sirius Red positive areas in the images, as shown in Figure 5G and H.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Despite its inhibitory effect on collagen 1 production levels, Chol-MCT1-siRNA did not reduce Sirius Red positive areas in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: Despite its inhibitory effect on collagen 1 production levels, Chol-MCT1-siRNA did not reduce Sirius Red positive areas.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: GN-MCT1-siRNA treatment caused comparable M1/M2 macrophage activation levels to Chol-MCT1-siRNA treatment in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: However, GN-MCT1-siRNA treatment caused comparable M1/M2 macrophage activation levels to Chol-MCT1-siRNA treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The opposite fibrotic phenotypes caused by the different siRNA constructs are not due to M1/M2 macrophage polarization.
source: These data suggest that the opposite fibrotic phenotypes caused by the different siRNA constructs are not due to M1/M2 macrophage polarization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing comparable M1/M2 macrophage activation.

claim: Successful depletion of hepatic stellate cell-selective Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA was confirmed in the MCT1fl/fl mice injected with the AAV9-Lrat-Cre construct.
source: Successful depletion of hepatic stellate cell-selective Slc16a1Mct1 mRNA was confirmed in the MCT1fl/fl mice injected with the AAV9-Lrat-Cre construct.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA levels in the hepatocytes were intact after AAV9-Lrat-Cre injection in MCT1fl/fl mice.
source: Slc16a1/Mct1 mRNA levels in the hepatocytes, which account for up to 70% of total liver cell types, were intact (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: No change in MCT1 protein level was observed in other metabolic tissues after AAV9-Lrat-Cre injection in MCT1fl/fl mice.
source: No change in MCT1 protein level was observed in other metabolic tissues (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: CDHFD induces severe steatosis due to inhibited VLDL secretion and β-oxidation and thereby exacerbates NASH fibrosis in a relatively short time.
source: CDHFD induces severe steatosis due to inhibited VLDL secretion and β-oxidation and thereby exacerbates NASH fibrosis in a relatively short time (Raubenheimer et al., 2006; Matsumoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raubenheimer et al., 2006; Matsumoto et al., 2013.

claim: There was no food intake or body weight difference between the groups of MCT1fl/fl mice on CDHFD with different AAV treatments.
source: There was no food intake or body weight difference between the groups (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: MCT1 deletion in either hepatocytes or in hepatic stellate cells did not resolve steatosis in MCT1fl/fl mice on CDHFD.
source: Similar to the results we obtained by MCT1 silencing with siRNAs (Figure 4), MCT1 deletion in either hepatocytes or in hepatic stellate cells did not resolve steatosis (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Hepatocyte-specific knockout of MCT1 (Hep KO) enhanced the collagen 1 level compared to the control group in MCT1fl/fl mice on CDHFD.
source: Also consistent with the results obtained by hepatocyte selective MCT1 silencing with GN-MCT1-siRNA (Figure 5), hepatocyte-specific knockout of MCT1 (Hep KO) enhanced the collagen 1 level compared to the control group (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Hepatic stellate cell-specific MCT1 knockout (HSC KO) prevented CDHFD-induced collagen 1 protein levels in MCT1fl/fl mice.
source: In contrast, hepatic stellate cell-specific MCT1 knockout (HSC KO) prevented CDHFD-induced collagen 1 protein levels (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7B.

claim: MCT1KO in combined hepatocytes and hepatic stellate cells blunted the effect shown in each single KO in MCT1fl/fl mice on CDHFD.
source: MCT1KO in combined hepatocytes and hepatic stellate cells blunted the effect shown in each single KO (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Overall liver fibrosis detected by trichrome staining confirmed the acceleration of fibrosis in the Hep KO group in MCT1fl/fl mice on CDHFD.
source: Overall liver fibrosis detected by trichrome staining again confirmed the acceleration of fibrosis in the Hep KO group and a downward trend in the HSC KO group (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Overall liver fibrosis detected by trichrome staining showed a downward trend in the HSC KO group in MCT1fl/fl mice on CDHFD.
source: Overall liver fibrosis detected by trichrome staining again confirmed the acceleration of fibrosis in the Hep KO group and a downward trend in the HSC KO group (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Dual MCT1KO in hepatocytes plus hepatic stellate cells showed no change in overall fibrosis in MCT1fl/fl mice on CDHFD.
source: Dual MCT1KO in hepatocytes plus hepatic stellate cells showed no change in overall fibrosis, similar to the Chol-MCT1-siRNA results (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Hep KO mice exhibited elevated liver stiffness over all other groups at 4 weeks of the CDHFD.
source: After 8 weeks of CDHFD, all groups had the same level of increased liver stiffness above what the control mice showed at 4 weeks, however, Hep KO mice exhibited elevated liver stiffness over all other groups at 4 weeks of the diet (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: After 8 weeks of CDHFD, all groups had the same level of increased liver stiffness above what the control mice showed at 4 weeks.
source: After 8 weeks of CDHFD, all groups had the same level of increased liver stiffness above what the control mice showed at 4 weeks, however, Hep KO mice exhibited elevated liver stiffness over all other groups at 4 weeks of the diet (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: There was no change in plasma alanine transaminase (ALT) levels among the groups of MCT1fl/fl mice on CDHFD.
source: There was no change in plasma alanine transaminase (ALT) levels among the groups (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7H.

claim: No increase in collagen mRNA or protein levels upon lactate treatment was observed in LX2 cells.
source: However, no increase in collagen mRNA or protein levels upon lactate treatment was observed (Figure 8A and B), suggesting that lactate itself may not be a fibrogenic inducer.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Lactate itself may not be a fibrogenic inducer in LX2 cells.
source: However, no increase in collagen mRNA or protein levels upon lactate treatment was observed (Figure 8A and B), suggesting that lactate itself may not be a fibrogenic inducer.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no effect of lactate alone.

claim: The combination treatment of sodium pyruvate (1 mM) and sodium lactate (10 mM) significantly enhanced both mRNA and protein expressions of collagen 1 in LX2 cells treated with TGF-β1.
source: Interestingly, the combination treatment of sodium pyruvate (1 mM) and sodium lactate (10 mM) significantly enhanced both mRNA and protein expressions of collagen 1 (Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8C–E.

claim: MCT1 depletion in LX2 cells prevented TGF-β1-stimulated collagen 1 production in conditions where lactate was solely generated by endogenous glycolysis.
source: MCT1 depletion in LX2 cells prevented TGF-β1-stimulated collagen 1 production in both conditions where lactate was solely generated by endogenous glycolysis (Figure 8F) and where exogenous lactate was supplied (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8F.

claim: MCT1 depletion in LX2 cells prevented TGF-β1-stimulated collagen 1 production in conditions where exogenous lactate was supplied.
source: MCT1 depletion in LX2 cells prevented TGF-β1-stimulated collagen 1 production in both conditions where lactate was solely generated by endogenous glycolysis (Figure 8F) and where exogenous lactate was supplied (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Although lactate itself is not a fibrogenic inducer, it can assist in TGF-β1-induced collagen production via MCT1 in LX2 cells.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that although lactate itself is not a fibrogenic inducer, it can assist in TGF-β1-induced collagen production via MCT1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing lactate enhancement of TGF-β1 effects.

claim: MCT1-siRNA significantly decreased the phosphorylated SMAD3 (pSMAD3) protein level and the pSMAD3/SMAD3 ratio in the absence of TGF-β1 treatment in LX2 cells.
source: As a result, we observed that MCT1-siRNA significantly decreased the phosphorylated SMAD3 (pSMAD3) protein level and the pSMAD3/SMAD3 ratio in the absence of TGF-β1 treatment (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B), implying the potential regulatory effect of MCT1 on the TGF-β1-SMAD3 axis.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: MCT1 has a potential regulatory effect on the TGF-β1-SMAD3 axis in LX2 cells.
source: As a result, we observed that MCT1-siRNA significantly decreased the phosphorylated SMAD3 (pSMAD3) protein level and the pSMAD3/SMAD3 ratio in the absence of TGF-β1 treatment (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B), implying the potential regulatory effect of MCT1 on the TGF-β1-SMAD3 axis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing effects on SMAD3 phosphorylation.

claim: In the presence of TGF-β1 pretreatment, the contribution of pSMAD on MCT1's inhibitory effect on collagen 1 production was limited in LX2 cells.
source: Interestingly, however, in the presence of TGF-β1 pretreatment, the contribution of pSMAD on MCT1's inhibitory effect on collagen 1 production was limited.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: MCT1 depletion inhibited collagen production in LX2 cells, but the significant decrease of pSMAD3/SMAD ratio was only shown upon low concentrations of TGF-β1 (0, 1, 2.5 ng/ml) pretreatment.
source: While MCT1 depletion inhibited collagen production, the significant decrease of pSMAD3/SMAD ratio was only shown upon low concentrations of TGF-β1 (0, 1, 2.5 ng/ml) pretreatment (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Both SMAD3-dependent and independent MCT1 regulation may be relevant to the TGF-β1-induced collagen production.
source: This data suggests that both SMAD3-dependent and independent MCT1 regulation may be relevant to the TGF-β1-induced collagen production in which MAPK, NF-kB, and PI3K are potential mediators in SMAD3-independent TGF-β1 pathways (Derynck and Zhang, 2003; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data, supported by citations to Derynck and Zhang, 2003; Xu et al., 2016.

claim: MAPK, NF-kB, and PI3K are potential mediators in SMAD3-independent TGF-β1 pathways.
source: This data suggests that both SMAD3-dependent and independent MCT1 regulation may be relevant to the TGF-β1-induced collagen production in which MAPK, NF-kB, and PI3K are potential mediators in SMAD3-independent TGF-β1 pathways (Derynck and Zhang, 2003; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Derynck and Zhang, 2003; Xu et al., 2016.

claim: MCT1-siRNA treatment depleted SLC16A1/MCT1 mRNA levels in HepG2 cells.
source: MCT1-siRNA treatment depleted SLC16A1/MCT1 mRNA levels (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) and significantly enhanced fibrogenic gene markers ACTA2 and COL1A1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MCT1-siRNA treatment significantly enhanced fibrogenic gene markers ACTA2 and COL1A1 in HepG2 cells.
source: MCT1-siRNA treatment depleted SLC16A1/MCT1 mRNA levels (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) and significantly enhanced fibrogenic gene markers ACTA2 and COL1A1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HepG2-derived conditioned media-treated LX2 cells did not change the expression of fibrogenic genes.
source: However, HepG2-derived conditioned media-treated LX2 cells did not change the expression of fibrogenic genes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Enhanced fibrogenesis due to GN-MCT1-siRNA treatment of mice may be a direct effect of hepatocyte MCT1 depletion.
source: These data are consistent with the idea that enhanced fibrogenesis due to GN-MCT1-siRNA treatment of mice may be a direct effect of hepatocyte MCT1 depletion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing increased fibrogenic markers in HepG2 cells.

claim: Hepatic stellate cells are thought to be the primary producers of collagen, contributing 10–20 times more collagen than hepatocytes or endothelial cells, respectively, in rodent systems.
source: However, hepatic stellate cells are thought to be the primary producers of collagen, contributing 10–20 times more collagen than hepatocytes or endothelial cells, respectively, in rodent systems (Friedman et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Friedman et al., 1985.

claim: MCT1 function in hepatic stellate cells promotes collagen 1 expression.
source: The major finding of this study is that MCT1 function in hepatic stellate cells promotes collagen 1 expression, as MCT1 depletion in this cell type, either in vitro in cell culture (Figure 1B) or in vivo in mice (Figure 7B), attenuates fibrotic collagen 1 protein production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Lactate may enhance TGF-β1-induced collagen production via MCT1 in studies in cultured LX2 cells.
source: We also provided evidence that lactate may enhance TGF-β1-induced collagen production via MCT1 in studies in cultured LX2 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Previous use of Lrat-Cre for germline transmission had validated constitutive gene KO selectively in hepatic stellate cells in mice.
source: Previous use of Lrat-Cre for germline transmission had validated constitutive gene KO selectively in hepatic stellate cells in mice (Mederacke et al., 2013), while our AAV-Lrat-Cre construct allows inducible gene KO, eliminating time-demanding mouse crossing and breeding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mederacke et al., 2013.

claim: The AAV-Lrat-Cre construct allows inducible gene KO, eliminating time-demanding mouse crossing and breeding.
source: Previous use of Lrat-Cre for germline transmission had validated constitutive gene KO selectively in hepatic stellate cells in mice (Mederacke et al., 2013), while our AAV-Lrat-Cre construct allows inducible gene KO, eliminating time-demanding mouse crossing and breeding.
evidence: This is a methodological advantage of the AAV-Lrat-Cre construct developed in this study.

claim: MCT1KO in hepatocytes evoked a robust upregulation of collagen 1 expression and fibrosis.
source: Surprisingly, MCT1KO in hepatocytes, both in vivo (Figure 7A) and in vitro (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), evoked the opposite effect: a robust upregulation of collagen 1 expression and fibrosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Increased local lactate may enhance stellate cell collagen production after hepatocyte MCT1KO.
source: This may be an effect of increased local lactate to enhance stellate cell collagen production, but may also be in part a cell-autonomous effect in hepatocytes, as we observed increased collagen 1 expression in Hep2G cells upon silencing SLC16A1/MCT1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: Hepatocyte MCT1KO may have a cell-autonomous effect on collagen 1 expression in hepatocytes.
source: This may be an effect of increased local lactate to enhance stellate cell collagen production, but may also be in part a cell-autonomous effect in hepatocytes, as we observed increased collagen 1 expression in Hep2G cells upon silencing SLC16A1/MCT1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is speculation supported by experimental data showing increased collagen 1 expression in HepG2 cells.

claim: Lactate flux via MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells strongly promotes collagen 1 translation or inhibits protein turnover rates.
source: Nonetheless, taken together, our data suggest that lactate flux via MCT1 in hepatic stellate cells strongly promotes collagen 1 translation or inhibits protein turnover rates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The inhibitory effect of stellate cell MCT1KO was observed only at the collagen 1 protein level, while the hepatocyte MCT1KO affected both collagen mRNA and protein.
source: Interestingly, the inhibitory effect of stellate cell MCT1KO was observed only at the collagen 1 protein level, while the hepatocyte MCT1KO affected both collagen mRNA and protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Increased import of lactate into hepatic stellate cells may serve as a precursor for glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline synthesis.
source: The exact mechanism needs to be further investigated, but one possibility is that increased import of lactate into hepatic stellate cells serves as a precursor for glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline synthesis, as suggested in other systems such as cancer or pulmonary fibrosis (Pérez-Escuredo et al., 2016; Hamanaka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Pérez-Escuredo et al., 2016; Hamanaka et al., 2019.

claim: Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 silencing strongly upregulated collagen 1 in livers of ob/ob mice on a GAN diet.
source: Hepatocyte-selective MCT1 silencing strongly upregulated collagen 1 in livers of ob/ob mice on a GAN diet (Figure 5D–F), as did hepatocyte-selective MCT1KO in the CDHFD mouse model (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Chol-conjugated, chemically modified siRNA targeting MCT1 silenced the gene in all three liver cell types tested, including hepatic stellate cells.
source: In contrast, Chol-conjugated, chemically modified siRNA targeting MCT1 silenced the gene in all three liver cell types tested, including hepatic stellate cells (Figure 3E–G), and did attenuate liver collagen 1 expression (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Chol-conjugated, chemically modified siRNA targeting MCT1 attenuated liver collagen 1 expression in ob/ob mice on GAN diet.
source: In contrast, Chol-conjugated, chemically modified siRNA targeting MCT1 silenced the gene in all three liver cell types tested, including hepatic stellate cells (Figure 3E–G), and did attenuate liver collagen 1 expression (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Five RNAi-based therapeutic agents have received FDA approvals targeting multiple disease areas.
source: To date, five RNAi-based therapeutic agents have received FDA approvals targeting multiple disease areas, and a great many clinical trials of oligonucleotide therapeutics are in progress (Padda et al., 2023; Traber and Yu, 2023; Zhu et al., 2022; Mullard, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Padda et al., 2023; Traber and Yu, 2023; Zhu et al., 2022; Mullard, 2022.

claim: A great many clinical trials of oligonucleotide therapeutics are in progress.
source: To date, five RNAi-based therapeutic agents have received FDA approvals targeting multiple disease areas, and a great many clinical trials of oligonucleotide therapeutics are in progress (Padda et al., 2023; Traber and Yu, 2023; Zhu et al., 2022; Mullard, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Padda et al., 2023; Traber and Yu, 2023; Zhu et al., 2022; Mullard, 2022.

claim: Hepatic MCT1 positively regulates the levels of SREBP1 and ChREBP, major transcription factors regulating liver lipid metabolism, as well as their target DNL genes.
source: Analysis of gene expression profiles also showed that hepatic MCT1 positively regulates the levels of SREBP1 and ChREBP, major transcription factors regulating liver lipid metabolism, as well as their target DNL genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The effects of hepatic MCT1 on DNL genes were apparently not sufficient to reverse severe steatosis in the genetically obese NASH mouse model.
source: These effects were apparently not sufficient to reverse severe steatosis in the genetically obese NASH mouse model (Figure 4), although a slight decrease in mean lipid droplet size was observed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The remaining steatosis may be attributed to the continuous supply of fatty acids from adipose tissue lipolysis, which accounts for up to 65% of hepatic fat accumulation as opposed to only 25% coming from hepatic DNL.
source: The remaining steatosis may be attributed to the continuous supply of fatty acids from adipose tissue lipolysis, which accounts for up to 65% of hepatic fat accumulation as opposed to only 25% coming from hepatic DNL (Donnelly et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Donnelly et al., 2005.

claim: MCT1 haploinsufficiency showed greatly reduced HFD-induced hepatic steatosis.
source: However, since MCT1 haploinsufficiency showed greatly reduced HFD-induced hepatic steatosis, the discrepancies with our data may be due to other tissues being involved or the different mouse models used.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior literature.

claim: Steatosis is not much affected by hepatic MCT1 depletion in two models of NASH in mice.
source: Overall, it is clear from our studies that steatosis is not much affected by hepatic MCT1 depletion in two models of NASH in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: DGAT2 is effective in reducing steatosis when depleted.
source: A possible future strategy for NASH therapeutics may be to combine the depletion of MCT1 in stellate cells to decrease fibrosis with a potent anti-steatosis target such as DGAT2 (Yenilmez et al., 2022; Calle et al., 2021; Loomba et al., 2020) which we and others have shown is effective in reducing steatosis when depleted.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yenilmez et al., 2022; Calle et al., 2021; Loomba et al., 2020.

claim: Hepatic MCT1 silencing enhanced AMPK phosphorylation.
source: Indeed, hepatic MCT1 silencing enhanced AMPK phosphorylation, consistent with the previous MCT1 haploinsufficient mice study (Carneiro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, supported by citation to Carneiro et al., 2017.

claim: MCT1 inhibition reduced ATP production and activated AMPK, thus deactivating SREBP1c and lowering levels of its target SCD1.
source: These data are also in line with another study in which MCT1 inhibition reduced ATP production and activated AMPK, thus deactivating SREBP1c and lowering levels of its target SCD1 (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: Hepatic stellate cell MCT1 is a potential therapeutic target to prevent NASH fibrogenesis related to collagen 1 production.
source: In summary, the data presented here highlight hepatic stellate cell MCT1 as a potential therapeutic target to prevent NASH fibrogenesis related to collagen 1 production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The utility of hepatic stellate cell MCT1 as a therapeutic target is complicated by the finding that MCT1 depletion in hepatocytes actually increases fibrosis.
source: Its utility as a therapeutic target is complicated by our finding that MCT1 depletion in hepatocytes actually increases fibrosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: This work highlights the importance of contemplating cell-type specificity when developing therapeutic strategies, especially in systems of complex cellular landscapes such as NASH.
source: This work highlights the importance of contemplating cell-type specificity when developing therapeutic strategies, especially in systems of complex cellular landscapes such as NASH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.
